steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing a diffusion model for layout-to-image generation. Explain why text prompts are not enough for complex multi-object scenes, why GAN-based layout-to-image methods fall short, how our model fuses layout and image, and end with the experimental setting and a list of main contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Text-to-image diffusion and its limits for complex scenes; layout as guidance
- Prior layout-to-image work: GANs, and little use of diffusion
- Our design goals and why layout-image fusion is hard
- Our model: unified form, LFM, OaCA, fast sampling
- Experiments and main contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Text-to-image diffusion and layout guidance
  - diffusion progress in conditional generation, esp. text-to-image: GLIDE (cite), Imagen (cite), Stable Diffusion (cite)
  - failures (Fig. 1 (a)): complex multi-object images, hard to design prompt properly/comprehensively
  - even good prompts: missing objects, wrong positions, shapes, categories in SOTA text-guided models (cite)
  - cause: text ambiguity, weak at expressing position in image space (cite)
  - coarse layout = objects with bounding box (bbox) + category -> spatial + high-level semantics, controllability + high quality
- Prior work
  - early layout-to-image (cite) almost all GANs: unstable convergence (cite), mode collapse (cite)
  - diffusion: easy training (cite), big quality gains (cite), yet few studies on layout-to-image
  - only LDM (cite) supports layout condition
- Our design goals
  - LDM: simple multimodal fusion (e.g. cross attention) or direct input concatenation; we design layout-image fusion specifically
  - LDM conditions only in second stage; we: end-to-end one-stage, condition throughout -> may mitigate loss in fine-grained pixel-space tasks (cite)
  - layout-image fusion hard: more restrictions on position, size, category than text; needs higher controllability, hurts naturalness/diversity
  - layout sensitive to each token; lost token -> missing object
- Our model: LayoutDiffusion
  - patched image + layout in unified form; structural image patch at multi-resolution with region (position + size)
  - each patch = special object, whole patched image = layout -> simple fusion in same spatial space
  - Layout Fusion Module (LFM): fuse each object's info, model relations, latent of whole layout
  - object-aware Cross Attention Mechanism (OaCA): image patch feature x layout, unified coordinate space, positions as bounding boxes
  - classifier-free training and sampling; faster sampling, beats SOTA in 25 iterations
- Experiments and contributions
  - COCO-stuff (cite), Visual Genome (VG) (cite); quality, diversity, controllability; beats GAN- and diffusion-based SOTA
  - contributions: diffusion model for layout-to-image with precise position/size control; patches as objects, LFM + OaCA; FID, DS, CAS gains of around 46.35 \%, 9.61 \%, 26.70 \% (COCO-stuff) and 44.29 \%, 11.30 \%, 41.82 \% (VG)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recently, diffusion models have made encouraging progress in conditional image generation, especially in text-to-image generation, for example GLIDE, Imagen, and Stable Diffusion. But text-guided diffusion models can still fail in some situations. As Fig. 1 (a) shows, when we want to generate a complex image with multiple objects, it is hard to design a prompt that is proper and comprehensive. Even with well-designed prompts, the state-of-the-art text-guided diffusion models still have problems such as missing objects and generating the wrong positions, shapes, and categories of objects. This is mainly because text is ambiguous and it is weak at precisely expressing positions in the image space. This is not a problem when we use a coarse layout as guidance, which is a set of objects annotated with a bounding box (bbox) and an object category. With both spatial and high-level semantic information, the diffusion model can get more powerful controllability and still keep the high quality.

However, early studies on layout-to-image generation are almost all limited to generative adversarial networks (GANs), and they often suffer from unstable convergence and mode collapse. Diffusion models have advantages in easy training and give significant quality improvement, but few studies have applied diffusion to the layout-to-image generation task. As far as we know, only LDM supports layout as a condition, and it has shown encouraging progress in this field.

In this paper, unlike LDM, which uses a simple multimodal fusion method (e.g., cross attention) or direct input concatenation for all conditional input, we specifically design the fusion mechanism between layout and image. Also, instead of conditioning only in the second stage like LDM, we propose an end-to-end one-stage model that considers the condition for the whole process, which may help to mitigate loss in tasks that need fine-grained accuracy in pixel space. Fusing image and layout is a difficult multimodal fusion problem. Compared to fusing text and image, the layout puts more restrictions on the position, size, and category of the objects. This needs higher controllability from the model, and this often lowers the naturalness and diversity of the generated image. Also, the layout is more sensitive to each token, and losing a token of the layout directly leads to missing objects.

- Our design goals
  - unlike LDM (simple fusion such as cross attention, or direct concatenation): design layout-image fusion specifically
  - end-to-end one-stage, condition for the whole process (LDM only in second stage)
  - fusion hard: layout restricts position, size, category more than text; controllability vs naturalness/diversity; lost layout token -> missing object
- Our model
  - unified form: structural image patch at multi-resolution with region (position, size); patch = object, patched image = layout
  - LayoutDiffusion = LFM + OaCA + classifier-free training/sampling
  - LFM: fuse objects, model relations, latent of whole layout; OaCA: object-aware cross-attention in unified coordinate space
  - faster sampling, beats SOTA in 25 iterations
- Experiments: COCO-stuff, Visual Genome (VG); beats GAN- and diffusion-based SOTA
- Contributions
  - diffusion model for layout-to-image, quality + diversity + precise control
  - patches as special objects, LFM and OaCA
  - FID, DS, CAS gains: around 46.35 \%, 9.61 \%, 26.70 \% (COCO-stuff), 44.29 \%, 11.30 \%, 41.82 \% (VG)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recently, diffusion models have made encouraging progress in conditional image generation, especially in text-to-image generation, for example GLIDE, Imagen, and Stable Diffusion. But text-guided diffusion models can still fail in some situations. As Fig. 1 (a) shows, when we want to generate a complex image with multiple objects, it is hard to design a prompt that is proper and comprehensive. Even with well-designed prompts, the state-of-the-art text-guided diffusion models still have problems such as missing objects and generating the wrong positions, shapes, and categories of objects. This is mainly because text is ambiguous and it is weak at precisely expressing positions in the image space. This is not a problem when we use a coarse layout as guidance, which is a set of objects annotated with a bounding box (bbox) and an object category. With both spatial and high-level semantic information, the diffusion model can get more powerful controllability and still keep the high quality.

However, early studies on layout-to-image generation are almost all limited to generative adversarial networks (GANs), and they often suffer from unstable convergence and mode collapse. Diffusion models have advantages in easy training and give significant quality improvement, but few studies have applied diffusion to the layout-to-image generation task. As far as we know, only LDM supports layout as a condition, and it has shown encouraging progress in this field.

In this paper, unlike LDM, which uses a simple multimodal fusion method (e.g., cross attention) or direct input concatenation for all conditional input, we specifically design the fusion mechanism between layout and image. Also, instead of conditioning only in the second stage like LDM, we propose an end-to-end one-stage model that considers the condition for the whole process, which may help to mitigate loss in tasks that need fine-grained accuracy in pixel space. Fusing image and layout is a difficult multimodal fusion problem. Compared to fusing text and image, the layout puts more restrictions on the position, size, and category of the objects. This needs higher controllability from the model, and this often lowers the naturalness and diversity of the generated image. Also, the layout is more sensitive to each token, and losing a token of the layout directly leads to missing objects.

To solve these problems, we propose to treat the patched image and the input layout in a unified form. Specifically, we build a structural image patch at multi-resolution by adding the concept of region, which contains position and size information. This way each patch of the image becomes a special type of object, and the whole patched image can also be seen as a layout. Then the difficult multimodal fusion between image and layout becomes a simple fusion in a unified form in the same spatial space of the image. We call our model LayoutDiffusion. It is a layout-conditional diffusion model with a Layout Fusion Module (LFM), an object-aware Cross Attention Mechanism (OaCA), and a corresponding classifier-free training and sampling scheme. LFM fuses the information of each object and models the relationships between multiple objects, and it gives a latent representation of the whole layout. To make the model pay more attention to the information related to the objects, we propose an object-aware fusion module called OaCA. The cross-attention is done between the image patch feature and the layout in a unified coordinate space, by representing the positions of both of them as bounding boxes. To improve the user experience of LayoutDiffusion further, we also optimize the speed of the classifier-free sampling process, and the model could significantly outperform the SOTA models in 25 iterations.

We run experiments on COCO-stuff and Visual Genome (VG). Various metrics for quality, diversity, and controllability show that LayoutDiffusion significantly outperforms both state-of-the-art GAN-based and diffusion-based methods.

Our main contributions are listed below.

- Instead of the dominant GAN-based methods, we propose a diffusion model called LayoutDiffusion for layout-to-image generation, which generates images with high quality and diversity while keeping precise control over the position and size of multiple objects.
- We propose to treat each patch of the image as a special object and do the difficult multimodal fusion of layout and image in a unified form. We then propose LFM and OaCA to fuse the multi-resolution image patches with the user’s input layout.
- LayoutDiffusion outperforms the SOTA layout-to-image generation method on FID, DS, CAS by relatively around 46.35 \%, 9.61 \%, 26.70 \% on COCO-stuff and 44.29 \%, 11.30 \%, 41.82 \% on VG.

Even with well-designed prompts, the state-of-the-art text-guided diffusion models [1,3,2] still have problems such as missing objects and generating the wrong positions, shapes, and categories of objects. This is mainly because text is ambiguous and it is weak at precisely expressing positions in the image space [4,5,6,7,8,9]. This is not a problem when we use a coarse layout as guidance, which is a set of objects annotated with a bounding box (bbox) and an object category. With both spatial and high-level semantic information, the diffusion model can get more powerful controllability and still keep the high quality.

However, early studies [10,11,12,13] on layout-to-image generation are almost all limited to generative adversarial networks (GANs), and they often suffer from unstable convergence [14] and mode collapse [15]. Diffusion models have advantages in easy training [16] and give significant quality improvement [17], but few studies have applied diffusion to the layout-to-image generation task. In this paper, unlike LDM, which uses a simple multimodal fusion method (e.g., cross attention) or direct input concatenation for all conditional input, we specifically design the fusion mechanism between layout and image. Also, instead of conditioning only in the second stage like LDM, we propose an end-to-end one-stage model that considers the condition for the whole process, which may help to mitigate loss in tasks that need fine-grained accuracy in pixel space [3]. This way each patch of the image becomes a special type of object, and the whole patched image can also be seen as a layout. steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Recently, diffusion models have achieved encouraging progress in conditional image generation, especially in text-to-image generation such as GLIDE [1], Imagen [2], and Stable Diffusion [3]. However, text-guided diffusion models may still fail in the following situations. As shown in Fig. 1 (a), when aiming to generate a complex image with multiple objects, it is hard to design a prompt properly and comprehensively. Even with well-designed prompts, problems such as missing objects and incorrectly generated object positions, shapes, and categories still occur in state-of-the-art text-guided diffusion models [1,3,2]. This is mainly due to the ambiguity of text and its weakness in precisely expressing positions in the image space [4,5,6,7,8,9]. Fortunately, this is not a problem when using a coarse layout as guidance, i.e., a set of objects annotated with a bounding box (bbox) and object category. With both spatial and high-level semantic information, the diffusion model can obtain more powerful controllability while maintaining high quality.

However, early studies [10,11,12,13] on layout-to-image generation are almost limited to generative adversarial networks (GANs) and often suffer from unstable convergence [14] and mode collapse [15]. Despite the advantages of diffusion models in easy training [16] and significant quality improvement [17], few studies have considered applying diffusion to the layout-to-image generation task. To our knowledge, only LDM [3] supports layout as a condition and has shown encouraging progress in this field.

In this paper, different from LDM, which applies a simple multimodal fusion method (e.g., cross attention) or direct input concatenation for all conditional input, we aim to specifically design the fusion mechanism between layout and image. Moreover, instead of conditioning only in the second stage like LDM, we propose an end-to-end one-stage model that considers the condition for the whole process, which may help mitigate loss in tasks requiring fine-grained accuracy in pixel space [3]. The fusion between image and layout is a difficult multimodal fusion problem. Compared to the fusion of text and image, the layout places more restrictions on the position, size, and category of objects. This requires higher controllability of the model and often decreases the naturalness and diversity of the generated image. Furthermore, the layout is more sensitive to each token, and the loss of a layout token directly leads to missing objects.

To address these problems, we propose treating the patched image and the input layout in a unified form. Specifically, we construct a structural image patch at multi-resolution by adding the concept of region, which contains position and size information. As a result, each patch of the image is transformed into a special type of object, and the entire patched image is also regarded as a layout. The difficult problem of multimodal fusion between image and layout is thus transformed into a simple fusion with a unified form in the same spatial space of the image. We name our model LayoutDiffusion, a layout-conditional diffusion model with a Layout Fusion Module (LFM), an object-aware Cross Attention Mechanism (OaCA), and a corresponding classifier-free training and sampling scheme. In detail, LFM fuses the information of each object and models the relationships among multiple objects, providing a latent representation of the entire layout. To make the model pay more attention to object-related information, we propose an object-aware fusion module named OaCA, in which cross-attention is computed between the image patch feature and the layout in a unified coordinate space by representing the positions of both as bounding boxes. To further improve the user experience of LayoutDiffusion, we also optimize the speed of the classifier-free sampling process, which significantly outperforms the SOTA models in 25 iterations.

Experiments are conducted on COCO-stuff [18] and Visual Genome (VG) [19]. Various metrics covering quality, diversity, and controllability show that LayoutDiffusion significantly outperforms both state-of-the-art GAN-based and diffusion-based methods.

Our main contributions are listed below.

- • Instead of the dominant GAN-based methods, we propose a diffusion model named LayoutDiffusion for layout-to-image generation, which can generate images with both high quality and diversity while maintaining precise control over the position and size of multiple objects.

- • We propose to treat each patch of the image as a special object and accomplish the difficult multimodal fusion of layout and image in a unified form. LFM and OaCA are proposed to fuse the multi-resolution image patches with the user’s input layout.

- • LayoutDiffusion outperforms the SOTA layout-to-image generation method on FID, DS, CAS by relatively around 46.35 \%, 9.61 \%, 26.70 \% on COCO-stuff and 44.29 \%, 11.30 \%, 41.82 \% on VG.
